sections.title: Feline anemia and oxygen transport
paragraphs: Feline anemia reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. The clinical task is to restore effective oxygen transport while treating the cause of the anemia and managing circulation. Compatible donor blood remains central to feline transfusion care. [3,4]

Oxyglobin introduced a cell-free hemoglobin approach to this problem. The published feline record includes clinical series of 48 and 72 cats. These studies document hemoglobin responses, clinical observations and complications in patients receiving the historical carrier. [1,2]

sections.title: The 48-cat study
paragraphs: Weingart and Kohn reviewed 48 anemic cats treated between 2002 and 2006. The cats received 65 Oxyglobin infusions. Hemoglobin increased after 41 of the 49 infusion events with before-and-after measurements. The denominator is infusion events, not individual cats. [1]

Seven cats with cardiac disease developed serious adverse effects. Pulmonary edema occurred in five, pleural effusion in three and respiratory distress in one. The categories overlap. Four of these cats also received whole blood on the same day. Five died and one was euthanized. The authors identified circulatory overload as a major risk in cats with heart disease at the doses studied. [1]
Overall 24-hour survival was 77%. This was a retrospective clinical series without a randomized comparison group. The survival figure describes the treated population and its concurrent care. [1]

sections.title: The earlier 72-cat series
paragraphs: Gibson and colleagues reported 72 cats in 2002. Seventy received the carrier for anemia, commonly because compatible blood was unavailable. Improvements were recorded in 37 of the 43 more closely monitored cats. Adverse events were recorded in 44 of the full 72-cat cohort, and 23 cats were discharged. [2]

Pulmonary edema and pleural effusion were prominent complications. The authors identified infusion volume and rate as priorities for further investigation. Each clinical series has its own population and outcomes; the figures belong to those original groups. [2]

sections.title: PCV and hemoglobin measure different compartments
paragraphs: Packed cell volume measures the proportion of blood occupied by red cells. Cell-free hemoglobin circulates in plasma. An oxygen carrier can therefore change total hemoglobin without increasing red-cell volume. PCV remains a measure of the red-cell compartment. [3]

Effective oxygen delivery combines oxygen-carrying capacity with blood flow, oxygen binding and unloading, and tissue demand. Assessment needs to connect the blood measurement with the patient's physiology. [3]

sections.title: The feline development priorities for BHOC
paragraphs: BHOC, Biological Hemoglobin Oxygen Carrier, focuses on oxygen transport within Precision Oxygen Therapeutics. The feline development priorities are clear: characterize the formulation, assess cardiac status and circulating volume, measure oxygen-related responses, and track clinical outcomes. [4]

The Oxyglobin studies provide the historical clinical record. BHOC development takes these observations into a separate formulation-specific research program. The objective is effective tissue oxygen support with a defined safety profile. [4]
